## Dimension Reduction

This section identifies highly variable genes using robust variability measures, then uses principal components to summarize dominant structure in the expression matrix. The dimensional-reduction outputs here are exploratory and descriptive; the predictive PCA used for classification is fit later on the training data only.

```{python}
#| label: analyze-dimred-mad-pca-overview
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "PCA views based on genes selected by raw and log-scale MAD, followed by MAD distributions across genes."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
from scipy.stats import median_abs_deviation
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# =========================================================
# Setup
# =========================================================
X = df_gene_expr_by_sample.copy()

# =========================================================
# 1) Median Absolute Deviation for a single gene: ERBB2
# =========================================================
idx = pd.IndexSlice
erbb2_df = X.loc[idx[:, ["ERBB2"], :]]

vals = pd.to_numeric(erbb2_df.to_numpy().ravel(), errors="coerce")
vals = vals[np.isfinite(vals) & (vals > 0)]

mad_erbb2_raw = median_abs_deviation(vals, scale="normal")
mad_erbb2_log = median_abs_deviation(np.log1p(vals), scale="normal")

print("ERBB2 MAD (raw):", mad_erbb2_raw)
print("ERBB2 MAD (log1p):", mad_erbb2_log)

# =========================================================
# 2) MAD for all genes
# =========================================================
gene_mad_raw = {}
gene_mad_log = {}

for gene in X.index:
    vals = pd.to_numeric(X.loc[gene], errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    vals = vals[np.isfinite(vals) & (vals > 0)]

    if len(vals) == 0:
        gene_mad_raw[gene] = np.nan
        gene_mad_log[gene] = np.nan
    else:
        gene_mad_raw[gene] = median_abs_deviation(vals, scale="normal")
        gene_mad_log[gene] = median_abs_deviation(np.log1p(vals), scale="normal")

gene_mad_raw = pd.Series(gene_mad_raw, name="MAD_raw").dropna().sort_values(ascending=False)
gene_mad_log = pd.Series(gene_mad_log, name="MAD_log").dropna().sort_values(ascending=False)

top_genes_raw = gene_mad_raw.head(2000).index
top_genes_log = gene_mad_log.head(2000).index

# Optional: inspect top genes
print("\nTop 10 genes by raw MAD:")
print(gene_mad_raw.head(10))

print("\nTop 10 genes by log MAD:")
print(gene_mad_log.head(10))

# =========================================================
# 3) PCA using top genes selected by RAW MAD
#    PCA is done on log1p-transformed values for stability
# =========================================================
X_raw = X.loc[top_genes_raw].T
X_raw = X_raw.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
X_raw = np.log1p(X_raw)

scaler_raw = StandardScaler()
X_raw_scaled = scaler_raw.fit_transform(X_raw)

pca_raw = PCA(n_components=2)
X_pca_raw = pca_raw.fit_transform(X_raw_scaled)

print("\nExplained variance ratio (RAW MAD selection):", pca_raw.explained_variance_ratio_)
print("Total explained by PC1 + PC2 (RAW MAD selection):", pca_raw.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())

# =========================================================
# 4) PCA using top genes selected by LOG MAD
# =========================================================
X_log = X.loc[top_genes_log].T
X_log = X_log.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
X_log = np.log1p(X_log)

scaler_log = StandardScaler()
X_log_scaled = scaler_log.fit_transform(X_log)

pca_log = PCA(n_components=2)
X_pca_log = pca_log.fit_transform(X_log_scaled)

print("\nExplained variance ratio (LOG MAD selection):", pca_log.explained_variance_ratio_)
print("Total explained by PC1 + PC2 (LOG MAD selection):", pca_log.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())

# =========================================================
# 5) Build plotting data
# =========================================================
df_plot_raw = pd.DataFrame(
    X_pca_raw,
    index=X_raw.index,
    columns=["PC1", "PC2"]
).join(df_sample_meta[["SUBTYPE"]])

df_plot_log = pd.DataFrame(
    X_pca_log,
    index=X_log.index,
    columns=["PC1", "PC2"]
).join(df_sample_meta[["SUBTYPE"]])

df_plot_raw["SUBTYPE"] = df_plot_raw["SUBTYPE"].fillna("NA")
df_plot_log["SUBTYPE"] = df_plot_log["SUBTYPE"].fillna("NA")

# =========================================================
# 6) Plot side-by-side
# =========================================================
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True)

plot_info = [
    (
        axes[0],
        df_plot_raw,
        "Top 2000 genes by RAW MAD",
        pca_raw.explained_variance_ratio_
    ),
    (
        axes[1],
        df_plot_log,
        "Top 2000 genes by LOG MAD",
        pca_log.explained_variance_ratio_
    ),
]

for ax, df_plot, title, evr in plot_info:
    for subtype, group in df_plot.groupby("SUBTYPE"):
        ax.scatter(
            group["PC1"],
            group["PC2"],
            label=subtype,
            alpha=0.7
        )

    ax.set_title(
        f"{title}\nPC1={evr[0]:.2%}, PC2={evr[1]:.2%}",
        fontsize=11
    )
    ax.set_xlabel("PC1")
    ax.set_ylabel("PC2")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)

axes[1].legend(title="Subtype")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

axes[0].hist(gene_mad_raw, bins=50)
axes[0].set_title("MAD on raw values")
axes[0].set_xlabel("MAD")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Number of genes")

axes[1].hist(gene_mad_log, bins=50)
axes[1].set_title("MAD on log1p values")
axes[1].set_xlabel("MAD")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Median Absolute Deviation (MAD)**

MAD measures how much a gene varies across samples relative to its median value. It is computed as the median of the absolute deviations from the median.

A low MAD means the gene is relatively stable across samples. A high MAD means the gene varies more across samples and may therefore be more informative for distinguishing biological groups. MAD is useful because it is more robust to extreme values than variance or standard deviation.

**Why use log transform before or during selection**

mRNA expression data are often strongly right-skewed, with a small number of very large values. A log transform compresses the upper tail and reduces the influence of extreme values. This helps make variability measures and PCA focus more on pattern than on sheer magnitude.

**Explained Variance Ratio**

The explained variance ratio tells us how much of the total variation in the data is captured by each principal component. For example, if PC1 explains 25% of the variation and PC2 explains 12%, then the first two components together summarize 37% of the overall structure in the selected genes.

```{python}
#| label: analyze-dimred-scree-cumulative-comparison
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Scree plots and cumulative explained-variance plots highlighting three component choices: 2 PCs, the parallel-analysis choice, and the 95% cumulative explained-variance choice."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 12

X_log = X.loc[top_genes_log].T
X_log = X_log.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
X_log = np.log1p(X_log)

scaler_log = StandardScaler()
X_log_scaled = scaler_log.fit_transform(X_log)

n_components_fit = min(X_log_scaled.shape[0], X_log_scaled.shape[1])
pca_log_n_components = PCA(n_components=n_components_fit)
X_pca_log_n_components = pca_log_n_components.fit_transform(X_log_scaled)

evr = pca_log_n_components.explained_variance_ratio_
cum_evr = np.cumsum(evr)

# -------------------------------------------------
# Component choices
# -------------------------------------------------
k_min = 2

def parallel_analysis(X, n_iter=500, percentile=95, random_state=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)
    n, p = X.shape
    n_components = min(n, p)
    rand_eigs = np.zeros((n_iter, n_components))

    for i in range(n_iter):
        X_rand = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
        pca_rand = PCA(n_components=n_components).fit(X_rand)
        rand_eigs[i, :] = pca_rand.explained_variance_

    rand_threshold = np.percentile(rand_eigs, percentile, axis=0)
    return rand_threshold, rand_eigs

real_eigs = pca_log_n_components.explained_variance_
rand_thresh, rand_eigs_all = parallel_analysis(
    X_log_scaled,
    n_iter=500,
    percentile=95,
    random_state=42
)

k_parallel = int(np.sum(real_eigs > rand_thresh))
k_95 = int(np.argmax(cum_evr >= 0.95) + 1)

print("2 PCs:", k_min)
print("Parallel analysis PCs:", k_parallel)
print("95% cumulative explained variance PCs:", k_95)

# -------------------------------------------------
# Use the three choices directly
# Row 1: 2 PCs
# Row 2: parallel-analysis PCs
# Row 3: 95% EVR PCs
# -------------------------------------------------
k_values = [k_min, k_parallel, k_95]
row_titles = [
    f"2 Principal Components",
    f"{k_parallel} Principal Components",
    f"{k_95} Principal Components"
]

max_plot_k = max(k_values)
pcs = np.arange(1, max_plot_k + 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(12, 12))

green = "green"
old_color = "lightgrey"

for row_idx, k_current in enumerate(k_values):
    ax_scree = axes[row_idx, 0]
    ax_cum = axes[row_idx, 1]

    # ---------------------------------------------
    # Scree plot
    # ---------------------------------------------
    ax_scree.bar(pcs, evr[:max_plot_k])

    # previous selections in grey, current in green
    for k_prev in k_values[:row_idx]:
        ax_scree.axvline(
            k_prev,
            linestyle="--",
            linewidth=1.5,
            color=old_color,
            label=f"{k_prev} PCs"
        )

    ax_scree.axvline(
        k_current,
        linestyle="--",
        linewidth=2,
        color=green,
        label=f"{k_current} PCs"
    )

    ax_scree.set_title(f"{row_titles[row_idx]}: Scree Plot")
    ax_scree.set_xlabel("Principal Component")
    ax_scree.set_ylabel("Explained Variance Ratio")
    ax_scree.set_xlim(0.5, max_plot_k + 0.5)
    ax_scree.grid(alpha=0.2)
    ax_scree.legend()

    # ---------------------------------------------
    # Cumulative explained variance
    # ---------------------------------------------
    ax_cum.plot(pcs, cum_evr[:max_plot_k], marker="o", linewidth=1)

    # grey previous highlighted points
    for k_prev in k_values[:row_idx]:
        prev_idx = np.arange(k_prev)
        ax_cum.plot(
            pcs[prev_idx],
            cum_evr[prev_idx],
            marker="o",
            linestyle="None",
            color=old_color,
            label=f"First {k_prev} PCs"
        )

    # green current highlighted points
    curr_idx = np.arange(k_current)
    ax_cum.plot(
        pcs[curr_idx],
        cum_evr[curr_idx],
        marker="o",
        linestyle="None",
        color=green,
        label=f"First {k_current} PCs"
    )

    ax_cum.set_title(f"{row_titles[row_idx]}: Cumulative Explained Variance")
    ax_cum.set_xlabel("Principal Component")
    ax_cum.set_ylabel("Cumulative Explained Variance Ratio")
    ax_cum.set_xlim(0.5, max_plot_k + 0.5)
    ax_cum.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
    ax_cum.grid(alpha=0.2)
    ax_cum.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pca-cumulative-summary
#| echo: false

k_values = [k_min, k_parallel, k_95]

summary_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Number of PCs": k_values,
    "Cumulative Explained Variance": [cum_evr[k - 1] for k in k_values]
})

# optional: nicer formatting
summary_df["Cumulative Explained Variance"] = summary_df["Cumulative Explained Variance"].round(4)

summary_df
```

### Parallel Analysis

```{python}
#| label: analyze-dimred-parallel-analysis-monte-carlo
#| eval: true
#| output: true

def parallel_analysis(X, n_iter=500, percentile=95, random_state=None):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)
    n, p = X.shape
    n_components = min(n, p)
    rand_eigs = np.zeros((n_iter, n_components))

    for i in range(n_iter):
        X_rand = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
        pca_rand = PCA(n_components=n_components).fit(X_rand)
        rand_eigs[i, :] = pca_rand.explained_variance_

    rand_threshold = np.percentile(rand_eigs, percentile, axis=0)
    return rand_threshold, rand_eigs

seeds = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
k_values = []

for seed in seeds:
    rand_thresh, _ = parallel_analysis(
        X_log_scaled,
        n_iter=500,
        percentile=95,
        random_state=seed
    )
    k_parallel = np.sum(real_eigs > rand_thresh)
    k_values.append(k_parallel)

print(k_values)
print("min =", min(k_values), "max =", max(k_values), "mean =", np.mean(k_values))
```

Parallel analysis was performed using `n_iter = 500` Monte Carlo simulations. The selected number of components was checked for stability by repeating the simulation under multiple random seeds, and the resulting cutoff did not vary, indicating that the Monte Carlo approximation was adequate.




## Statistical Modelling

In this section we move from unsupervised structure discovery to supervised classification. The goal is not to optimize every modelling choice, but to complete a clean 80/20 modelling pipeline that is consistent with the assignment workflow: split first, fit preprocessing on the training data only, apply the learned transformations to the test data, then evaluate predictive performance.

### Important correction before modelling

The PCA code in the previous section fits PCA on the full dataset before any train/test split. That is acceptable for exploratory visualization, but it should not be used for predictive evaluation because the test set influences the principal component directions. For modelling, we must:

1. split the data into training and testing sets,
2. fit the scaler on the training data only,
3. fit PCA on the training data only,
4. transform the test data using the fitted training scaler and training PCA.

### Build an 80/20 train-test pipeline

```{python}
#| label: analyze-model-build-matrix
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, accuracy_score
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Build modelling matrix from the chosen high-variance genes
# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Uses the same variable selection decision already made above:
# top_genes_log = top 2000 genes by log-MAD

X_model = X.loc[top_genes_log].T.copy()
X_model = X_model.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
X_model = np.log1p(X_model)

# align subtype labels to the modelling matrix
# drop samples without subtype labels just in case

y_model = df_sample_meta.loc[X_model.index, "SUBTYPE"].copy()
valid_mask = y_model.notna()

X_model = X_model.loc[valid_mask].copy()
y_model = y_model.loc[valid_mask].copy()

print("X_model shape:", X_model.shape)
print("Subtype counts (full data):")
print(y_model.value_counts())
```

```{python}
#| label: analyze-model-train-test-split
# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 2) 80/20 split (stratified)
# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Replace this with your student number if you want assignment-style reproducibility.
SEED = 3660

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_model,
    y_model,
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=SEED,
    stratify=y_model
)

print("Training shape:", X_train.shape)
print("Testing shape:", X_test.shape)
print("\nTraining subtype counts:")
print(y_train.value_counts())
print("\nTesting subtype counts:")
print(y_test.value_counts())
```

### Fit the scaler and PCA on the training data only

```{python}
#| label: analyze-model-fit-training-pca
# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 3) Standardize using training data only
# ---------------------------------------------------------
scaler_train = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler_train.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler_train.transform(X_test)

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 4) PCA using training data only
# ---------------------------------------------------------
max_pcs = min(X_train_scaled.shape[0], X_train_scaled.shape[1])
pca_train = PCA(n_components=max_pcs)
X_train_pca = pca_train.fit_transform(X_train_scaled)
X_test_pca = pca_train.transform(X_test_scaled)

print("Training PCA shape:", X_train_pca.shape)
print("Testing PCA shape:", X_test_pca.shape)
print("Total explained variance from all training PCs:", pca_train.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())
```

@fig-model-training-pca-scatter shows the first two training-set principal components and is used only as a descriptive view of class separation in the training data.

    X_train_pca[:, :2],
    index=X_train.index,

).join(y_train.rename("SUBTYPE"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))

for subtype, group in train_pca_df.groupby("SUBTYPE"):
    ax.scatter(group["PC1"], group["PC2"], alpha=0.7, label=subtype)

ax.set_title(f"Training PCA: PC1 vs PC2\nPC1={ev_train[0]:.2%}, PC2={ev_train[1]:.2%}")
ax.set_xlabel("PC1")

ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
ax.legend(title="Subtype")

@fig-model-training-scree summarizes how much of the standardized training-set variation is captured by the first 25 principal components.

cum_evr_train = np.cumsum(evr_train)
pcs_25 = np.arange(1, first_n + 1)

### Choose a reasonable number of PCs for multinomial logistic regression

We will use a simple, defensible heuristic rather than hyperparameter tuning. The “one in ten” rule is not a theorem, but it is a conservative screening device for avoiding an overly large model relative to the smallest class. We therefore combine the parallel-analysis suggestion with a class-size cap and use the smaller value for the main model.

```{python}
#| label: analyze-model-pc-choice
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 7) Define the three PCA comparison choices
# ---------------------------------------------------------
n_min_train = y_train.value_counts().min()

# minimum comparison model
k_min = 2

# reuse training-PCA quantities
evr_train = pca_train.explained_variance_ratio_
cum_evr_train = np.cumsum(evr_train)

# parallel-analysis choice from earlier section
try:
    k_parallel_model = int(k_parallel)
except NameError:
    raise ValueError("k_parallel is not defined. Run the training-based parallel analysis first.")

# 95% cumulative explained-variance choice
k_95_model = int(np.argmax(cum_evr_train >= 0.95) + 1)

# keep values within valid bounds
max_valid_pcs = X_train_pca.shape[1]
k_min = min(k_min, max_valid_pcs)
k_parallel_model = min(k_parallel_model, max_valid_pcs)
k_95_model = min(k_95_model, max_valid_pcs)

k_values_to_compare = [k_min, k_parallel_model, k_95_model]
k_values_to_compare = list(dict.fromkeys(k_values_to_compare))  # preserve order, remove duplicates

print("Smallest training subtype count:", n_min_train)
print("k_min:", k_min)
print("k_parallel:", k_parallel_model)
print("k_95:", k_95_model)
print("Component counts to compare:", k_values_to_compare)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-model-pc-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Three PCA dimension choices used for multinomial logistic-regression comparison."

pc_summary_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": ["Minimum", "Parallel analysis", "95% cumulative explained variance"],
    "Number of PCs": [k_min, k_parallel_model, k_95_model],
    "Cumulative Explained Variance": [
        cum_evr_train[k_min - 1],
        cum_evr_train[k_parallel_model - 1],
        cum_evr_train[k_95_model - 1]
    ]
})

pc_summary_table["Cumulative Explained Variance"] = (
    pc_summary_table["Cumulative Explained Variance"].round(4)
)

pc_summary_table
```

### Fit multinomial logistic regression models

To keep the workflow simple, we compare three models:

- a minimal model using the first 2 principal components,
- a model using the number of components selected by parallel analysis,
- a model using the smallest number of components needed to reach 95% cumulative explained variance.

Because the subtype classes may not be perfectly balanced, we use `class_weight="balanced"` so that smaller classes are not ignored during fitting.

```{python}
#| label: analyze-model-helper-functions-inline
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 8) Helper functions for fitting and evaluation
# ---------------------------------------------------------
def fit_multinomial_logit(X_train_pca, y_train, n_pcs):
    model = LogisticRegression(
        solver="lbfgs",
        class_weight="balanced",
        max_iter=5000,
        random_state=SEED
    )
    model.fit(X_train_pca[:, :n_pcs], y_train)
    return model


def evaluate_model(model, X_pca, y_true, labels):
    y_pred = model.predict(X_pca)
    acc = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    misclassification_rate = 1 - acc
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=labels)
    cm_df = pd.DataFrame(cm, index=labels, columns=labels)
    return {
        "accuracy": acc,
        "misclassification_rate": misclassification_rate,
        "confusion_matrix": cm_df,
        "predictions": y_pred,
    }
```

labels = sorted(y_train.unique())

model_results = {}
results_rows = []

for k in k_values_to_compare:
    model = fit_multinomial_logit(X_train_pca, y_train, k)
    res = evaluate_model(model, X_test_pca[:, :k], y_test, labels)

    model_results[k] = {
        "model": model,
        "results": res
    }

    results_rows.append({
        "model": f"{k} PCs",
        "n_components": k,
        "accuracy": res["accuracy"],
        "misclassification_rate": res["misclassification_rate"]
    })

results_table = pd.DataFrame(results_rows).sort_values(
    ["misclassification_rate", "n_components"],
    ascending=[True, True]
).reset_index(drop=True)

results_table

### Interpretation

At this stage, we are not trying to optimize the final classifier. Instead, we want a complete and coherent modelling pipeline that respects the training/testing split and lets us compare downstream conclusions under a fixed sequence of decisions.

The most important modelling lesson here is that PCA belongs inside the training pipeline when the goal is prediction. Exploratory PCA on the full dataset is useful for visualization, but predictive evaluation must keep the test set isolated until the very end.



## Conclusions

This project shows that high-dimensional analysis is best understood as a sequence of linked decisions rather than as a single isolated method. The data used here are already the product of prior biological and computational processing, which means that interpretation requires attention to provenance, normalization, identifier handling, feature selection, dimensional reduction, and modelling.

The final modelling section therefore emphasizes a defensible workflow rather than aggressive optimization: the train/test split is established first, preprocessing is learned on the training data only, PCA is treated as part of the predictive pipeline, and results are summarized using held-out performance and confusion patterns.

Substantively, the main conclusion is not that one single classifier or transformation is universally best, but that downstream conclusions depend on the whole analytical pipeline. Methodologically, the document argues for explicit assumptions, reproducible setup, and careful separation between exploratory analysis and predictive evaluation.


The document therefore supports a cautious substantive claim and a stronger methodological one: in high-dimensional genomics, what we conclude depends not only on the observed data, but on the sequence of preprocessing and modelling decisions used to turn those data into evidence.
